opus-5.5.text:
I think much further than most people assume. That's one of the most interesting open questions in computer science.

In Go there are something like 10 to the 170 possible board positions, more than there are atoms in the universe. Brute force is hopeless. Protein folding looks just as intractable: a typical protein could take an astronomical number of shapes. Yet nature folds proteins in milliseconds, and AlphaGo found brilliant moves while searching a tiny fraction of the game tree. So how is that possible?

My conjecture is that the structures we care about in the natural world aren't random. They were shaped by evolution, physics, or geological processes, and so they have learnable regularities. If you build a model that captures those regularities, you can search the space intelligently instead of exhaustively. You only explore the small fraction of paths that are actually promising. That's what the neural network does in AlphaGo: it gives you a strong prior over moves and an evaluation of positions, so search becomes tractable.

So I'd put it this way: any pattern that can be generated or found in nature can potentially be efficiently discovered and modeled by a classical learning algorithm. If that's even roughly true, it has big implications. It would mean many problems we thought needed quantum computers, like certain quantum chemistry or materials simulations, might be approximated well enough by classical systems that learn the underlying dynamics.

I'm not saying quantum computing isn't important. It will be, especially for genuinely quantum systems with no exploitable structure. But I think we haven't come close to the limits of what classical Turing machines can do when you pair them with learned models of the world. AlphaFold was a kind of proof point for that, and I'd love to see how far it goes, maybe even toward simulating a whole virtual cell one day. In a way it touches the P versus NP question, too: maybe "hard" problems become much more approachable when the instances you care about come from a structured, natural distribution.

r001.rationale: The response says learned regularities can make search tractable for structured problems, but it does not propose polynomial-time search.

r002.rationale: It argues that AlphaGo and AlphaFold show classical computers can do much more than most people assume.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it can take us a very long way. My view—and it's been an informal thesis of mine for a long time—is that any pattern or structure that can be generated or found in nature can be efficiently discovered and modeled by a classical learning algorithm. Because the way we think about these problems is, you have this enormous combinatorial space—in Go, it's more positions than atoms in the universe; in protein folding, Levinthal's paradox, something like 10 to the 300 possible conformations—and brute force is hopeless. But the point is, nature doesn't brute force these things either. A protein folds in milliseconds. So there must be some structure to the landscape, and if there's structure, you can learn a model of that structure and use it to guide your search so you only have to look at a tiny fraction of the space.

That's really what AlphaGo did. The policy network and the value network are essentially a learned model of the dynamics of the game—what's promising, what's a good position—and that collapses the search tree into something tractable. And with AlphaFold we did something analogous, learning the physics and the evolutionary constraints implicitly from data rather than simulating every atom.

Now, the interesting question is where the limits of that are. There are things like quantum chemistry, simulating electron behavior precisely, where people assume you'd need a quantum computer. And maybe for some of those you do. But I actually think that boundary is further out than most people expect. We've done work on modeling the electron density with neural networks—approximating the Schrödinger equation—and you get surprisingly far. So my intuition is that a lot of what's thought to be only accessible via quantum computing may turn out to be learnable classically, because the systems in nature that evolved or formed did so with structure we can exploit.

Where it might break down is genuinely random or chaotic systems with no learnable regularities—there you can't do better than brute force. But I'd argue most of the problems we actually care about—materials, drug design, fusion plasma control, climate—aren't like that. They have structure. So I think of this as a general recipe: find a problem where you have a good simulator or a lot of data, where there's a clear objective, and where the search space is huge—and then learn the model and search. I think that recipe will carry classical computing much further than people assume.

r001.rationale: The candidate says learned models can make search tractable and examine a tiny fraction of the search space, but it does not communicate the specific claim that search becomes polynomial-time for a broad class of problems.

r002.rationale: The candidate argues that AlphaGo, AlphaFold, and neural-network modeling show classical computing can go much further than people assume.

astra-6.text:
I think it can take us a very long way. A lot of problems look intractable if you approach them by enumerating every possibility. Go is a good example: you’re never going to search the entire tree of possible games. But you don’t need to. You need to recognize which possibilities are promising and spend your computation there.

There’s a small distinction I’d make, though. In AlphaGo, the rules and dynamics were known; what we learned was how to guide the search and evaluate positions. With AlphaFold, we learned something about the relationship between a protein’s sequence and its structure. We weren’t simulating the whole folding process step by step. That’s part of what makes this approach so powerful: sometimes you can learn the answer to a question without reproducing every intermediate event in the underlying system.

The interesting question is how much structure there is in the problems we care about that we haven’t yet exploited. My intuition is that there’s an enormous amount. The problems nature presents us with aren’t necessarily the worst-case instances that make a computational problem hard.

That doesn’t mean learning removes fundamental computational limits. And there may be quantum systems for which a quantum computer really is the right tool. But I think we should be quite ambitious about finding out how far classical computation, guided by learning, can go. We’re a long way from exhausting that.

r001.rationale: The response says learning can focus computation on promising possibilities, but it does not claim this makes search polynomial-time for a broad class of problems.

r002.rationale: The response expresses optimism about how far learning-guided classical computation can go, but it does not say AlphaGo or AlphaFold demonstrated greater classical-computer capabilities than previously expected.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can take us a very long way. One of the things that’s fascinating about both Go and protein folding is that the space of possibilities is far too large to search exhaustively. So you have to learn something about the structure of the problem—what’s worth considering, what you can safely ignore—and use that to guide the computation.

Now, that doesn’t mean you’ve removed the underlying computational complexity. You haven’t suddenly made every hard problem easy. But the problems we care about in the real world often have structure. They’re not arbitrary instances of the worst possible case. And learning can exploit that structure in ways that our hand-designed algorithms may struggle to capture.

So I suspect there’s an enormous amount still to unlock with classical computers, especially by combining learned models with search and simulation. There will be limits, of course. Simulating quantum systems may be an area where you ultimately want a quantum computer. But even there, the interesting question is how far a learned approximation can get you for the particular thing you want to predict. I don’t think we know the limits of that yet.

r001.rationale: The response says learning can exploit problem structure to guide computation, but it does not claim this makes search polynomial-time for a broad class of problems.

r002.rationale: It predicts substantial untapped potential for classical computers, but does not argue that demonstrated AI achievements show classical computers are more capable than previously expected.
